[h1]STAR WARS™ - Knights of the Old Republic™[/h1] – [b]Adventure/RPG; Squad Tactics[/b]
[i]a spoiler-free review[/i]

[b]Rating:[/b] [i]Recommended as Essential[/i]


You wake up on a battle cruiser during an all-out firefight, find your way to the escape pods when it gets severely damaged, fight your way through enemy soldiers and crash-land on an unfamiliar planet. [u]Knights of the Old Republic[/u] [KOTOR] takes place some 4,000 years before the events of A New Hope; Yoda, Darth Vader, Obi-Wan Kenobi and Luke Skywalker are names of no consequence in the Star Wars universe. You are in completely new, unfamiliar territory here.

Star Wars fan or not, KOTOR is a game that everyone should play. A companion system ahead of its time, multiple storylines, rich dialogue and backstory, [b]YELLOW[/b] lightsabers and a unique tactical approach to combat allow this installment in the Star Wars series of games to really shine.

[b]- Companions -[/b]
You will meet several unique, diverse characters in your travels; a few of them can join your party. Grab two party members of your choice and your main character and hit the streets (or dunes, or forests, or whatever). These characters come with set attributes and skills, but when they level up (yes, there is a leveling/experience system; this is an RPG), you control how they improve.

[b]- Story -[/b]
No spoilers here, don’t worry. There are a multitude of side-quests to complete that complement the main quest, backstories to explore for each of your party members, fascinating lore on the origins of a few prominent species and multiple storylines. Depending on dialogue decisions, you can earn either Light Side or Dark Side points, determining the final path your story takes.

[b]- Cons -[/b]
Not too many of note. I clipped through the floor a couple times. A number of seemingly random fatal crashes. This game was put out in 2003, so it’s a little behind the times in visuals and the cutscenes are [i]really[/i] cheesy. The camera is a bit tricky to figure out at first. If you’re not expecting tactical battles (give orders rather than do battle yourself), it can be quite confusing. The biggest thing is that your companions will, at times, slow down or stop when you’re not looking for no reason, preventing you from entering the next area.
[u]The Bottom Line:[/u] None of these presents anything more than minor frustration; the game is well-built.

Well, that’s all I have to say about KOTOR. An aged but timeless classic that any Star Wars fan (and quite a few non-Star Wars fans) will enjoy.

Your father's favourite Star Wars title. This is the game of a true Star Wars fan. Not as clumsy or random as an EA title; an elegant game for a more civilised age. 

For over 30 years, LucasArts were the guardians of quality and integrity in the Star Wars universe. Before the dark times... before Disney. 


What rarity it is to have such an immersive experience - this game is simply a masterpiece in design and story-telling. I've not played this game on Steam in any meaningful way, but 20 years ago I played this game from start to finish and it has stayed with me ever since. I don't know of a single game that ever affected me so deeply or profoundly as this one. The characters and story were exceptionally well written and compelling, and all of it taking place in a universe I cherished and loved. 

I weep over the fall of Star Wars - from the grand and lofty heights that this title represented, to the brutalised corpse of an IP that now lay before us.

Enjoy this game, and remember a better time that was Star Wars.

This is the most frustrating game I've ever played and that's because it hates modern hardware.

First I booted the game and everything was stuck in 800x600 and I couldn't go to windowed mode. Okay cool, found out there's a patcher so I installed that and replaced my .exe and now I can play in 1920x1080 windowed, awesome!

Then I make my character, get into combat, and as soon as it ends I can't move my character. Do some searching, find out any framerate above 72FPS causes your traversal script to break. Okay, download rivatuner and set the FPS cap to 72FPS.

Awesome, seems to be going great, I play for 6 hours straight with no issues and beat Taris. Oh no, in the undercity there's black textures streaking across my screen and preventing progress. Okay, let's google, oh apparently having grass of all things enabled causes the bug. Disabled grass, all works fine.

Get to the Ebon Hawk. Pause and save my game, I'll play tomorrow.

Tomorrow comes, try loading my game from the main menu, every single save crashes on load. Search around, the only fix is to delete everything in the "currentgame" and "futuregame" folders, start a new game then load your game from the in-game pause menu. I do that, and it works, but now I have to do that every single time I play the game because the fix for disabling pause buffer and soft shadows doesn't work on it.

Now I'm on Kashyyyk and loading into exteriors crashes the game, look online, you need to run in compatibility mode for Windows XP SP2. Do that, works fine now. Waiting on the next inevitable issue.

And another issue cropped up a day later, I quicksaved and the game crashed at the same time, corrupting my quicksave entirely. Fortunately, I had a manual save from 20 mins before, but man that took the wind out of my sails.

Another thing that likes to happen is sometimes your ally and player AI breaks: you can start a fight, but your two companions stand still and are locked onto the enemies but wont do anything. You can solve this with quicksaving then quickloading, but it got me killed a few times.

I feel like I've worked 4 hours doing tech support just to play this thing but I loved this game. I beat it on the Xbox years ago but only remember the plot twist.  Despite my headaches, I do recommend this game, but be prepared for some major headaches ironing out all the compatibility issues you'll face. Even if you're not a Star Wars fan, which I don't consider myself either, this game as an RPG is one of the best and you can see a lot of the DNA that carried over into Mass Effect. All in all, if we judged this game as a product of its time, it's easily a 10/10 and likely worked out of the box back then. Judging it by modern hardware standards, it's an 8/10 due to the tedium of getting everything to cooperate, but once it does, you get one of the best Star Wars games and RPGs ever made. I never felt restricted to one path, I played light at first, then I turned to the Dark Side on Korribaan but the game allowed me to redeem myself which I chose to do after Juhani gave me a speaking to. That kind of flexibility is absent in a lot of modern games, even BioWare's own.  KotoR really lives up to its reputation of being one of the best games ever made. I hope Steam gives it the same treatment KotoR 2 got so it works better for future players.

A flawed masterpiece.

KOTOR is set thousands of years before the original trilogy when Darth Malak is on the verge of wiping out the republic, a short while after the Mandalorian wars. I think this is an excellent setting, as it frees the plot and characters from any limits the movie canon may have imposed. The setting is also built very well. I had no prior knowledge of the mandalorian wars or anything related, and bit by bit, npcs you talk to feed you enough information to piece it all together. 

This is an rpg in the style of classic pen and paper rpgs, like dnd. This means pretty much everything in the game is a stat check revolving around a d20 roll that can have positive or negative modifiers that help or hinder your chances.

Unfortunately, this is where the game first makes a mistake, presenting stats and this explanation during character creation. The game does a fine job of telling you what each stat does, but in classic rpg fashion, upon first playing the game you have absolutely no idea how relevant each stat will be. They're not all equal, I'll tell you that much. 

I got pretty far with my first playthrough, maybe a third of the way through the game, a bit less, when I realized I had completely destroyed my character. I had not fed points in correct amounts across the stats I needed, and as a result, my character missed attacks constantly, was hit almost every time, and while trash encounters were alright, any boss encounter would totally serve me. I started over after doing some research on character building. I recommend you do, too.

This is especially important because this game has classes that prioritize different stats. There are three base classes, Soldier, Scout, and Scoundrel, and three Jedi classes, Guardian, Sentinel, and Consular. I have only done one playthrough, as a Scout Consular, so I can't speak to the validity of other classes or how fun their playstyles are. Scout is the jack of all trades between a beat-em-up soldier and a stealth based scoundrel. Consular is all force power spam, all the time. I had a ton of fun with Consular, although you want to select your force powers carefully. As a Consular, you get one for each level up, the most of all the Jedi classes, and will only be able to fill out a portion the forcepower tree. This is probably the time that it's fair to mention that I went with a darkside playthrough. Normally I'd address this only in the story, but your alignment is a stat in this game. The further you are on one side, the cheaper the force powers of those side are to cast, and the more expensive the other side is. As a sith, this meant I had almost no light side powers, and pretty much used all darkside powers. I had cure, and speed, all others were darkside powers.

Combat is turn based, but it's all fully animated and the game doesn't autopause for you, you have to do that, so it feels less like turn based combat. That's nice for me, because I normally hate turn based combat, and in this game I can watch my dudes wackity wack the baddies (or often goodies in my case). And yes, not dude, dudes. You get companions in this game. In fact, you get a whole roster of FULLY FLESHED OUT CHARACTERS. You can have up to two accompanying you at any time. There are a few spots in the game where you are forced to play solo, but these are few and far between, and not difficult in my experience. I cannot tell you how amazing it is to have such beautifully written characters as your companions at all time. I don't have a lot more to say about gameplay except for my problems with the game that I'll get to at the end. So, story time.

The story in this game is very, very good. My only complaint with it is the black and white nature of the morality and the light and dark side, although, to be fair, this is probably a complaint to take up with star wars as a whole rather than this particular game. Even so, this is to the game's detriment so I need to call it out. I think it would be less common in a light side playthrough, but on a darkside playthrough, things just felt goofy sometimes. This is mostly due to the companions. There is a heavy sway towards all of the companions being light side. There are nine of them, and only two are dark side, while one is neutral (but honestly he has a heart of lightside even tho he's a cranky boy). 

This doesn't seem like a problem at first, because hey, two dark side companions, two companion slots, perfect! Well, not so much. Both dark side companions are basically blaster wielding soldiers. Swords at a stretch. That means if you want ANY force power support, you need a light side jedi companion. For most of the game, I had Bastila and HK-47 accompany me. HK-47 is a dark side combat droid that is an enthusiastically childish psychopath. He loves blowing brains out, and I love to indulge him. He is the funniest part of this game, and made a huge difference in the quality of my playthrough. Don't leave him behind, even if you're going light side. Bastila, however, is a good two shoes jedi, and this is where we get back to the goofy writing.

I'm a sith, okay? That means I'm going to intimidate everyone and abuse my force powers to get what I want. Usually, money or lower prices, sometimes extra goodies. Bastila hates this, and everytime I do it she reprimands me. This is, in part, actually amazing. Your companions will jump in on your conversations and add their two cents. It enhances the experience so much, but it gets comically laughable when I blatantly ignore Bastila's constant remarks about my behavior. Made funnier that, no matter what, she will still follow me into combat. Oh, well. 

I think I'm sounding more harsh than I really feel. That's a minor nitpick, really, the story to this game is phenomenal. Even though my playthrough was darkside, being selfish and all, I could not help but get emotionally attached to my companions and their experiences, and that is so, so powerful. That magnified the power of the last few hours of the game tenfold, it made the experience so rich. It is not often that I play a game with characters this fleshed out, and it shows.

I have one major complaint, honestly, about this game, and that is some of the final combat encounters leading up to the final boss. It's not infinite spawning enemies, but it's pretty darn close, and it's just frustrating as hell, and sent me into the ending of the game feeling pretty annoyed, and I think that impacted my experience. The ending was also not great. Totally meh. I was playing a sith, so what do I expect, but still, I feel like there's a lot of room for improvement.

This game rocks. Get it. Do your research. It also sucks on modern systems. I didn't play with mods, you should.

Gameplay: 9/10
Story: 10/10
Graphics: 8/10 (for the time)
Performance: 9/10

Overall: 9/10

When Star Wars fans talk about the Expanded Universe, this should be the first video game that comes to mind (this and the Jedi Knight series). Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic (nicknamed KOTOR) is an RPG that uses the d20 system and takes place approximately 4,000 years before the events of Star Wars: A New Hope while also predating the prequel movies. You won't encounter characters like Yoda, Obi-Wan, Luke Skywalker or Han Solo. Those characters weren't even born at this point. Instead, an entirely new cast of characters are presented to you, with their own personalities and backstories. In addition to a captivating story that parallels aspects of the movies, complete with a stunning twist.

Most Star Wars fans have played KOTOR at some point. Its hard to call someone a Star Wars fan, if they have never played or even heard of KOTOR. While a dated game by today's standards, KOTOR's story will have you fully immersed in the galaxy far, far away. You will encounter several recognizable locales, names and references from the Star Wars movies, but as explained previously, events will occur long before the movies. But the purpose of the Star Wars Expanded Universe has always been expanding on already established movies and allowing you to fully immerse yourself in the Star Wars universe. 

KOTOR's visuals are dated, but for the time it was released, they were considered state of the art. I highly recommend viewing various guides that exist that will allow higher resolutions, in addition to various graphical mods that can update the archaic visuals. But even so, I'm personally fond of the dated look as the game was intended. 

Performance for KOTOR is good for the most part. You may or may not experience issues depending on your hardware, but KOTOR is not a difficult game to run, and many guides exist that may help you to get the game running properly. Sound design is also well done. The soundtrack was composed by the well acclaimed Jeremy Soule (composer of Skyrim, Oblivion and Neverwinter Nights soundtracks as well).

[h1] “A Long Time Ago, in a Galaxy Far, Far Away…” [/h1]

A war rages between The Republic and The Sith. ‘Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic’ throws you head first into a fantastic recreation of the Star Wars universe filled with lightsabers, Sith Lords, and political intrigue, in an immersive, gripping tale of Good vs. Evil which - more than a decade on - stands tall as one of the best RPG’s of its generation, and probably the finest gaming interpretation of the iconic Star Wars franchise.

[b][u]Campaign:[/u][/b] Released in 2003 by Bioware | Lucas Arts, and set 4000 years before the events in ‘Star War’s - Episode 1: The Phantom Menace’, ‘SW:KOTOR’ tells the tale of a relative unknown caught up in events of cosmic proportions. The opening credits thrust you into the midst of an inter-galactic battle between Republic forces and a Dark Sith Lord, which finds you crash landing onto an alien planet, trying to stay alive and escape an inter-planetary Sith blockade. An unusually strong connection with the Force catapults the player from by-stander to protagonist, as an engaging, story-fueled campaign takes you across the galaxy from the mysterious water-world of Manaan, to the desert planet of Tatooine among many others. A lovingly crafted universe is filled with lots of recognizable faces to include – the treacherous Hutt’s, Bounty Hunter’s, Sith, Jedi Knights, Wookies, Protocol Droids, Rancor’s, and Sand People - amongst a broader cast of nearly 300 distinctive alien races.

[b][u]Gameplay | Graphics | Sound:[/u][/b] A Third-Person RPG in the classic mold, gameplay in ‘SW:KOTOR’ is built around the 4 pillars of ‘Character Development and Customization’, ‘Inventory Management’, ‘Combat’, and ‘Dialogue-driven Story-Telling’. You choose to play as one of three character classes (Soldier, Scout or Scoundrel – with both male and female options available), and then as one of three Jedi sub-classes (Sentinel, Consular or Guardian). A deep inventory system allows you to customize and equip your character with a multitude of clothing, weapon and armor options as well as assign XP to level-up in a variety of areas from Attributes, Skills, Feats, and Force Powers. Combat is based around the ‘D20’ RPG rule-set popularized in ‘Dungeons and Dragons (D&D)’, and while round-based, players are able to queue up actions and run them simultaneously in real-time. Finally, Character interaction is via a dialogue menu that is rumored to contain over 2000 lines of text, clearly geared toward maximizing player choice across multiple playthrough’s. While the broad strokes are seemingly representative of standard RPG fare, three elements serve to distinguish this title from the rank and file – 1.  The ability to switch to | customize | play as any character in your group provides for great overall variety 2. The campaign is well-paced with ‘Third Person’ gameplay broken up by ‘Rail-shooting’, ‘Stealth’, ‘Racing’, and ‘Gambling’ mini-games and 3. Deep customization options, lots of side-quests and the sheer glee of roaming the Star Wars universe adds great replayability to this title. Sound Design is also particularly noteworthy, with voice-acting, sound effects and background score composition all top-shelf. Well optimized K&M controls round out a well polished title.

[b][u]Flaws:[/u][/b] There is little to gripe about here, and perhaps the game’s biggest ‘flaw’ is its dated graphics - which have not aged particularly well - but it’s a testament to the overall strength of this title that it remains not only playable, but immensely engaging, despite this. Other minor issues include somewhat repetitive combat, and some minor character pathfinding issues.

Overall, ‘Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic’ is an erstwhile classic from another time, rich in Star Wars lore, with a deep, engaging campaign, a fantastic background score, compelling combat mechanics, high replayability and filled with iconic characters, plot twists, and moral complexities. This is a title you could easily lose yourself in for 50-60 hours on a single-playthrough, and that’s even before player-choice dictates your ultimate path to the Light or Dark Side. The Force is all around you, Padawan. What is your Destiny? – Highly Recommended! – (Rating 9/10)

Before Mass Effect there was Knights of the Old Republic. Bioware, in 2003, decided to introduce a decision-making system which enabled you, the player, to align yourself with either the light or the dark side. Major plot decisions could be made and your gender could also yield different options during the conversations.

This is one of the things one can like in KotOR. The two different alignments enable you to have at least two different playthroughs. But you have many side missions anyway. Even the companions can give you some. 

The world where the game takes place in shows us the previously unknown history of the Star Wars universe. A world that is 4,000 years before the films are taking place. You are awaken on a ship that is being attacked by Darth Malak. Your job is to escape, find companions, regroup and annihilate your archenemy. Of course, in the process you get to learn the Jedi way!

Do note that the game is round-based. You pick the actions necessary (though this is limited each round) and you can even pause at certain points. You can also make a decision on behalf of your companions - the choice is really yours. What I have found out about the game later on is that it is based on Dungeons and Dragons rules. And the actions are calculated in accordance with these rules. As to how successfully the dice were rolled and what modifications were applied to the damages you are not told - but this is accessible from a menu.

The game has excellent music (composed by Jeremy Soule), a long-lasting experience and, well, I wanted to say good graphics, but as the game has aged in the last 10 years or so, this is not really true anymore. Still, the art design is as Star Wars-esque as it can get and this being a Bioware RPG I highly recommend it. Not just for Star Wars fans or Bioware fans but to everybody wanting to have a good time!

[h1]This review is based on a purely vanilla playthrough[/h1]

+ Character creation allows stat customizations right from the get-go, and goes the extra mile by adding a 'recommended' button that offers balanced numbers based on class; useful feature for beginners
+ Very even and agreeable pace throughout the entirety of the game; never felt too fast, slow, or interspersed with filler content
+ Excellent, marvelous soundtrack; really keeps you in the game, and does well to make this title feel true to the franchise
+ Mercifully short load times
+ There are myriad available side-quests, all voiced
+ Combat mechanics are well thought-out (despite 'dice-roll' RNG, of which I am not normally fond, as a general rule) and give you plenty of room for creativity and finesse
+ Excellent story with lots of depth and freedom of choice
+ While some characters remained a bit two-dimensional throughout the game, the majority of them are adequately fleshed-out and seem to develop to some extend
+ The game includes a few optional minigames (eg. Pazaak Cards)
+ Multiple endings, based entirely around the player's decisions
+ Tons and tons of lore-friendly set-pieces and items (both practical and aesthetic)
+ Extremely, alarmingly mod-friendly
+ An absolute plethora of immersive dialogue options
+ Boasts a few masterful plot twists

- Poor camera; you get used to it, but it's initially quite frustrating and limited in functionality
- Poor inventory system; throws everything into one long list as you accumulate items, leading to lots of monotonous scrolling when looking for equipment (mostly a problem for fellow hoarders, you could just sell all of your junk)
- Mostly flat, uninspired voice-overs (some voice actors were of inordinately better quality, though that mostly served to highlight the disparity)
- AI movement is mostly terrible, leading to waiting for characters to catch up, and lots of blocked doors/paths
- Lots and lots of bugs and glitches; most notably terrain glitches and a few CTDs (some of this can be fixed with a small amount of modding, I'm told)
- The autosave function is too sparse in functionality, and has led to some extremely frustrating moments

When I went to college, my parents and grandparents bought me a laptop to do schoolwork on. I immediately ordered a copy of KOTOR for PC, this time springing for a new, unused copy. As if through divine intervention, I got an email saying KOTOR was ported to mac, I immediately downloaded steam on my mom's Macbook and purchased KOTOR on the spot. More than 20 years have passed since its initial release yet the critically acclaimed Star Wars: KOTOR remains one of the best Star Wars games ever made. With Bioware at the helm, already veterans of several previous RPG's, KOTOR is a role-playing game with a turn based combat system. Set 4000 years before the events of the movies, after the conclusion of the Mandalorian War, the Sith and Jedi are embroiled in conflict. We begin as a lowly soldier, with no memory of previous events, but one who we soon discover has force potential. Not only is this an exceptional story, one that could have easily made one of the greatest Star Wars films, but the freedom of choice truly augments the essence of this tale with incredible twists and turns.

Choices matter and will shape the direction that the story unfolds as well as influence the fate of the galaxy. Players can choose to follow the light or dark paths, which heavily determines relationships with our companions and even our appearance. Said companions come from varied backgrounds but hold many attributes of classic Star Wars characters. Most of them are distinct and quite memorable. The various worlds, likewise, are unique in setting and feature their own challenges and quests. The music flawlessly captures the Star Wars feel, with sweeping orchestral themes. The original KOTOR has what I believe is the quintessential "Star Wars experience" out of all the franchise games released to date. Mixing the gold-standard Bioware gameplay and character arcs before they became overused and predictable, a focus on exploration and discovery, respect to the SW lore and a strong attention to world-building and detail, it's a game that still stands the test of time and is recommended for any fan of RPGs.

As much as I'm a fan of KOTOR II's cerebral, relationship-driven, "take every trope and turn it on its head" gameplay, I still think the first game is the better of the two. The mystery of who you are, what your relationship is to the squadmates and enemies you meet in the world and how you grow to encompass that reputation again (whether for good or evil) still sticks out in the post-KOTOR world of cookie-cutter games like Bioware's own The Old Republic, which only has a superficial understanding of the choice and consequence that went into the former.

The plot is fairly straightforward. You are an amnesic man (or woman) who wakes up aboard a starship, having been out for several days and coming to just as it is being attacked by the Sith. Narrowly escaping with pilot Carth Onasi, your pod crashlands on the city-world of Taris, where you begin investigating the circumstances that led to your foggy memory. Along the way, you'll pick up a starship (the Ebon Hawk) and meet crew members like the murder-happy HK-47 assassin droid, Jedi Masters Bastila Shan, Juhani and Jolee Bindo, Mandalorian soldier Canderous Ordo and Wookie renegade Zaalbar, among others. All this comes to a head as you uncover the true identity of the Sith leader Revan and assault a space station called the Star Forge in order to stop Darth Malak, the man who took up Revan's job and threatens to destroy the galaxy.

This game has some of the most "pure" Star Wars moments I can think of. The moment when you first step out into the Dune Sea, and see that vista all around you and the smoldering Sandcrawler in the distance. The trek through to the lowest levels of Kashyykk and the civil war going on between the various Wookie factions. The underwater walks under Manaan. The reveal of Revan, backed by that epic score.

While the player being Darth Revan is a plot twist that is firmly in "It Was His Sled" territory as far as spoilers go, it didn't diminish my enjoyment of the game one bit despite knowing about it long beforehand. There's so much content to see and do that it really felt like an enjoyable and fulfilling role-playing experience. Whether it's doing some of the sidequests (like getting involved in ruling family squabbles or doing assassination contracts) or just running through some of the areas, there's a wealth of material here for fans.

It's true that the storyline wanes a bit by the end (not counting the potential Dark Side twists like convincing Zaalbar to kill Mission or the Bastila reveal), but it still didn't mar my enjoyment, mainly because I brought a pair of squadmates specced out for long-range combat (Canderous and Juhani) and went in guns-a-blazing in the Star Forge.

The morality system can also be exploited to great effect (you can get to full Light Side or Dark Side in less than half of one playthrough), including doing things like maxing out your LS points than choosing Bastila's Dark Side option at the end to still remain "neutral" but get her as a squadmate for the Star Forge finale.

If there's one thing I hated about the game, it's the inventory system. You WILL pick up a lot of vendor trash in this game, and I found it was far easier just to dump or never pick up most of the gear I found, sticking to one weapon until I found something significantly better.

It's also much better to spec your character manually, because the auto-level system is nigh-useless and will often result in your character gaining abilities that either aren't class-specific or generally have no benefit to you.

Regardless, KOTOR (and its sequel) still stand out among the best sci-fi RPG's in recent years, and the price point is a steal, regardless of whether it's on sale or not. If you haven't played it, you owe it to yourself to check this out.

So good! I was skeptical about the gameplay when I used to watch videos of this game but it works really well. 
You have 20 levels to rank up jedi powers, combat skills and feats (your starting class determines which of these 3 categories gets the most points per level up). A jedi power available is force lightning, a combat skill is something like flurry which increases your number of attacks but they deal less damage and might not hit and a feat is which type of armour you can wear or other passive benefits.
Combat is played on a turn-based dice roll system which might sound off-putting but works out well. Throughout the game you will meet characters who join you on your spaceship and you may choose 2 of them to accompany you outside of the ship. Companions will have their own stats, gear and skills so you can play around this (if you come across a companion with high lockpicking you might choose not to level your own and swap to this companion to unlock things for you). You can choose to level up your companions skills manually or automatically. 
You can choose preset combat manoeuvres for yourself and companions such as ranged attacking or jedi support (buffs and heals) or you can choose to manually decide you and your parties actions by pausing the combat and assign attacks and items to a queue. You also don't have to use companions at all, you can elect to play in a solo mode where all the exp gained from enemies will go straight to your character. You also don't have to worry about this mode because companions will automatically be boosted to your level if you haven't used them.
How you play the game is up to you. I went for a dual-lightsaber character with light armour and attack bonus jedi powers but you can play as a sniper, explosives expert, jedi caster or even unarmed fighting. 
The story is really what made the experience for me however. You will travel to multiple planets, gain your own starship, meet interesting characters and get to interact with almost every NPC you come across with multiple lines of dialogue and character development. 
One downside to this game is that you can't play in a widescreen resolution without using mods (although guides can be found for this on the forums here on steam, along with HD mods and many others).

Ahh KOTOR... I'd reckon any moderately passionate PC gamer growing up in the early 2000s will have played this one, or at least heard of it. For me, it's the very embodiment of childhood gaming. I've dumped hundreds of hours into this game as a kid... I even have the original 4-disk installation set sitting in my apartment somewhere, all scratched to hell from well over a decade of use. 

KOTOR stands as one of the defining fathers of story-driven RPGs that still holds up today, and for good reason: it's atmospherically beautiful, with a refreshing new soundtrack, a new-yet-familiar universe, interesting characters, multiple combat & skill paths, and a ton of small, subtle world-building details. Seriously, after over a decade and a half of playing this thing, I'm still bumping into lines of dialogue I haven't heard before. It also features one of the best (for the time, anyway) plot twists of any RPG, and a kick ass endgame & boss fight.

Let me say for the record that, while the remainder of the review will likely be filled with gripes, they should in no way deter you from picking this game up, if you don't have it already. Any true PC gamer should seriously consider getting this game, if nothing else for its historical impact on gaming history, and how to create a successful story-based RPG. I'd also like to say that, in comparison to KOTOR 2, this one's definitely got better polish & atmospherics, but the sequel has far greater gameplay depth & character development. Both are fantastic in their own rights though.

Right, so KOTOR is great, but not without flaws. Primarily, I find it's game mechanics substantially shallower than KOTOR 2's. Combat, character influence, and general balance between the various classes can be wildly inconsistent at times. To summarize: 
-Stealth is 100% useless and should never be invested into by any character class
-Sentinels & skill-based classes get screwed a bit because bypassing locks or hacking terminals has limited effectiveness, often only saving small amounts of time, but demanding huge skill investments with little rewards besides extra XP. Skilling/sabotage opportunities don't always show up consistently, and can have stupidly high costs associated with them (ex. corrupting droid targeting for a single room, vs disabling all droids on the map for a cheaper cost). Repairing droids has never made any difference in my games beyond the XP gains. Additionally, all Jedi classes get massive reductions to skill point gain, meaning that there's this weird transition between naturally gaining skill point levels, to relying entirely on boosting items, which usually means a big drop in combat potential (unless you like constantly swapping between skilling & combat items)
-Persuasion is similarly an all-or-nothing skill: if you don't invest a bunch of traits & skill points into it at game start, and keep actively investing in it, you'll find that the game will consistently outpace you with constantly growing skill check increases. Sentinels again get screwed in this department, being hard-locked into a slower skill gain, despite being the most skill-focused class available. Even then, most of the time persuasion skill checks just give you money without forcing you to use the more dark-side-focused intimidation options
-Stacking strength is honestly a little too powerful and nullifies some of the subtlety & appeal of the other classes. Hit ratios are absolutely abysmal in the early & mid games without high strength modifiers, and in most cases, chopping people up is typically a more effective solution than trying to bypass the problem via skills. It also completely nullifies gun-based characters, who get limited weapon choices and no damage modifiers from dexterity or items (and yes, I have attempted a few gunslinger main characters who used the force... it's an awful combination, don't try it)
-Duel-wielding is always way more optimal than single-bladed combat... in every scenario, for every build. The small defensive gains from single-bladed approaches are immediately nullified when as soon as you can customize a good offhand sword/lightsaber
-Some force powers are massively impactful, while others are nearly useless. Speed and Insanity are god-tier powers that can help carry even bad builds to victory... the latter by stunlocking entire rooms, and the former by being a massive time saver & allowing you to cheese solo fights more easily (attacking, then running away just before the animation finishes and denying enemies their retaliation turn)

Melee-using Soldiers and combat-classes dominate the meta. They're good from chapter 1 and remain strong the entire game, bypassing most problems with more consistent brute force tactics. The force jump ability is also insane in terms of combat movement and time saving. 
Sentinels are okay but don't have nearly the same impact as KOTOR 2 variants, mostly due to the fact that skill usage requires huge investment for minimal rewards. They're jankier than the other classes, becoming a sort of "jack of all trades, master on none" type that you can easily brick without careful skill & trait investment
Councilors are interesting but totally ineffective early game, requiring early trait investments for abilities you don't unlock until mid game (IE. Wisdom is wholly useless until you get force powers). Additionally, only dark side users can effectively make use of damage-based force builds... light side users are pretty much wholly relegated to stunning & buffing. 

In short, there's a lot of character building pitfalls one can accidentally step into, and it's very easy to start with, or transition into, a gimped character class that struggles the entire game. But on the flip side, a properly built one can obliterate the entire game with little contest.

That's mostly my gripes with the game. General lack of companion growth & feedback, especially compared to KOTOR 2, are the only other real gripes I can think of. Some companions will randomly switch what they believe in (ex. darker/"evil" companions can grow a sudden sense of misplaced honour at certain actions for no reason), and even if they vehemently disagree with you, their opinions typically don't carry over beyond single conversations. Light-side characters will always follow you even if you're a complete maniac, and will rarely step in to stop you, at least until the main endgame choices come along. None of the other characters beyond Carth and Bastila really change or develop much either, again comparing to the sequel where your companions will follow or reject you based off your decisions & opinions. Money's also a bit too easy to gain/cheese from both swoop circuits and selling items to the Yavin shop for way higher prices, cheapening a lot of the small, morality-focused "money vs piety" choices you make along the way. Character pathing is also pretty painful for most areas that aren't flat & wide-open, especially when using Speed powers.

Again though, all these gripes shouldn't distract from the fact that KOTOR is incredible game that should be a must-buy for all serious PC gamers. Atmospherically it's still way ahead of its time, and the moment-to-moment gameplay isn't hampered too badly by the occasionally combat and character-building flaws. The story's still kick ass, the planets are hugely memorable, and the endings are fantastic. 

Give this one a go, you'll almost certainly have a good time. Just be sure to look up some good character builds first.

This is not only the game that got me into Bioware, but it might be my first RPG I actually tried to get good at and learn the mechanics of; setting the oath for my love of RPG's as a whole. It's not perfect and it can be argued if it aged well or not, but it's a lot of fun to play and has a great story if you let it suck you in.

The game itself follows the tried and tested D&D rules like many Bioware games, with this game using a variation of 3rd/3.5 Edition rules; at least that's what it reminded me of. Put simpler; Dexterity for guns, Strength for melee. Feats add to abilities, skills and the like and force users essentially get a magic bar and the choice of powers every few levels. There's also the use of the ever present Dark side/Light side choice in Star Wars. This is mainly to affect opinions of your team mates in some conversations, but it also provides cheaper Force use for certain powers if they coincide with your alignment (Spamming Lightning never became easier!). It's nice simple, it works. There are a few useless powers and feats, but really, that's subjective on my part and there's probably someone out there for every combination.

As for the atmosphere and world building, I won't go into too much detail. It's Bioware, by this point we all know that Bioware can excel at this. I will say though that by being set years before the movies, there's a nice chance to set up some new villains and situations that provide a nice background to everything; I'd say the whole story is a huge point in the games favour.

Like I said though, the games not perfect. It's hard to ignore that the levels you visit are essentially successions of corridor after corridor. There's one path that reaches the end, sometimes you divert off it for secrets, but the path is always there. The game tries to disguise this, and I admit, it took me a while to catch on, but it's there, and hard to ignore once you notice. Not to mention, without spoiling it, the end game can feel a little sloggish with how it handles itself. It can be fun, but your first time, without expecting it, prepare for a lot of reloads.

Still, despite all that, the game's a tonne of fun to play and I love to return to it once in a while. I'd easily say it's worth every penny and should be played by everyone at least once; wholeheartedly reccomended

First, let me start by saying don't be deceived by my play time on Steam.  I have hundreds of hours in this game, if not more.  I own this game on XBOX, Android and even a physical copy of the game for PC.  However, my current gaming PC doesn't have a disc drive, so I decided to buy this version.

The game itself is a fantastic one, the story is wonderful and well written.  The characters are dynamic and there is a lot to do.  If you do full completion with all story and side quests, you'll spend many hours in this game.  And, it can be played again with a different character class, different gender and/or different choices made as far as light side and dark side choices, different gear, powers, etc., leading to a large number of combinations for different play throughs.  The graphics are really good, especially for 2002 standards, and the game is fully voice acted.  You can't run the game in widescreen without a patch, but you can set your anti aliasing and texture anistrophy pretty high, so the graphics hold up pretty well.  Combat is real time with pause, though it still maintains the roll system of a proper RPG.  Some of the quests in the game require force, while others are puzzles that have to be solved.  Also, unlike modern RPGs, there are no flashing signs or map markers telling you where to go, you simply have to figure it out.  The game is also pretty open world, especially after you do a couple planets and get freedom of movement in your starship.

Now for the Steam port.  Don't be fooled by the negativity, this is a good port.  When I first loaded the game, I turned up pretty much everything in the graphics settings to maximum and created my character.  Once I hit "Play," the game crashed.  So, I reloaded the game and went into the Advanced Graphics options and disabled "Frame Buffer Effects."  After that, no crashing.  I was able to create my character and I've been playing the game.  That's all it takes to get this game running.  So, it's not a bad port, people simply don't know this and think it's one, so they leave a bad review.

To summarize, this is one of the best games ever and it runs great on modern computers.  Get it.

What I Loved:
- Story
This game has one of the best stories that I have ever experienced in a game, easily standing next to some of the more modern greats. A timeless story of redemption and morality wrapped up in the Star Wars universe that has inspired so many stories and people before it. If you're a fan of story driven games that let you make your own decisions, especially the earlier Bioware works, then this game will not disappoint. This story has such heart & soul poured into it that I haven't seen matched in a Star Wars game until last year's Fallen Order.

- Characters
A story is often only as good as it's characters. In this game you have both.
The characters in this story are some of the best and well written characters I have experienced. Standouts for me would definitely be Bastila, Carth, Jolee, HK-47 along with Darth Revan & Malak. The first time I played through this game I loved these characters so much that I drowned myself in lore for weeks after so I could absorb as much as possible about them. They are timeless companions in the story that do more than just stand in the background in combat, they actively impact the story and the decisions you are called on to make. Characters like these make you give a damn about them and their fates and come along rarely. To have so many in one game is truly an achievement of the writers.

- Setting
Kotor is set thousands of years before the movie series and in my opinion is far better in every way. The Old Republic setting is at both times completely unique and familiar to Star Wars fans. It has its own lore, own characters, own planets. Its like a universe within a universe, one that's not so tied down by run time or budgets like the films. It can be as deep and imaginative as you want it to be and remains an untapped well for future instalments.

- Music
I could rave about the soundtrack of this game for days! Created by the one & only Jeremy Soule (greatest Video Game composer ever!) it offers a deep emotional impact to the scenes and worlds, never once feeling repetitive or uninspiring. Every piece of music feels unique and matches perfectly to the tone of whatever it is playing for. I've often played the soundtrack to this game in the background in the years since first playing it, its that good. What's truly great about it is that it never just recycles John Williams' score to the films. It's the Old Republic's own sound that is at both times Star Wars and it's own.

- Morality
Star Wars has always been a very cut and dry universe. The bad guys are bad, the good guys are good. What really amazes my about this game is that its very easy to feel conflicted over which choice is good or bad. Many morality systems in games are painfully straightforward and bland, Kotor makes choices feel like choices. You can understand why the opportunity to turn on the good guys would be appropriate. You can understand why betraying certain characters for the sake of others is both right and wrong at the same time. It offers you so much more depth to the choices than simply being good for the sake of being good or bad just because you feel like it. The first time I ever played this game in my teens I had to turn it off when I came to one of the final decisions because I couldn't decide which way I wanted to go with it and which characters I cared most about.

What I didn't like:
(Very LIttle. Honestly there is not much about this game that I didn't like or that I feel i couldn't look past.)
- Technical
There are the occasional hiccups that appear in the game such as sometimes getting stuck on geometry or something but I never experienced anything game breaking. A simple toggle to another character or autosave load would fix any small issue I came across. I never had any issues with crashing, objects disappearing, loading freezes, nothing at all. Considering the state of many modern games I think its unfair to even really say it has any. I only put this because I have heard of other people running into technical problems but I myself have never had any.

- Graphics
This can be an issue or not considering how forgiving you are to older games. I personally feel like the graphic are lacking compared to later games but considering it came out in 2003 and was made by a small team I think you can cut it some slack. The graphics are perfectly servicable and often have a charm all their own.

- Customisation
A lot of the game equipment is largely useless or impersonal. A lot of the armour is restricted to companions only as it hinders the player character in the use of force powers. All ranged weapons and melee weapons besides a lightsaber become obsolete after the first of seven worlds which can be a bit of a let down, particularly if you've put skill points into the use of these weapons. Character customisation is limited to a selection of default heads and what equipment IS useful to you is often very basic looking or reused models. The biggest example of this is that the best jedi robes in the game (besides those found before the final boss) and the worst robes have the exact same appearance. Which is also the same appearance as those worn by one of the companions and a few NPCs.


Overall I think everyone who considers themselves a gamer or a Star Wars fan should experience this game. For less than £10 for 30+ hours of very fun gameplay and an amazing storyline you can't go wrong.

STAR WARS Knights of the Old Republic 1 (KOTOR 1) is universally celebrated as a milestone in gaming history and one of the greatest role-playing games ever made. It provides the quintessential, cinematic "Star Wars fantasy" that lets you rise from a mysterious Republic soldier to a powerful Jedi Knight (or Dark Lord of the Sith). 

🌌 Pros: The Ultimate Star Wars Epic
- Iconic, Cinematic Storytelling: The narrative captures the grand scale of the original film trilogy, culminating in one of the most legendary, jaw-dropping plot twists in video game history.
- Unforgettable Companions: From the sarcastic bounty-hunting droid HK-47 to the noble Jedi Bastila Shan, the Ebon Hawk's crew is incredibly distinct, witty, and rich with deep backstories.
- Exceptional World Building: Exploring pre-Empire versions of iconic worlds like Tatooine, Kashyyyk, and Korriban four thousand years before the movies feels both fresh and nostalgic.
- Pure Star Wars Power Fantasy: The game flawlessly translates the d20 tabletop rules into a real-time-with-pause combat system, making constructing your first lightsaber and unlocking Force powers feel uniquely rewarding.

⚠️ Cons: What to Keep in Mind
- Dated 2003 Engine: The base animations, menus, and low-polygon characters show their age.
- Steam Compatibility Flaws: The game is notoriously difficult to run flawlessly on modern Windows 10/11 machines out of the box, frequently requiring community workarounds for crashes, broken resolutions, and movie-playback bugs.
- Sluggish Opening Planet: Taris, the massive multi-layered city world where you spend the first 5–8 hours of the game without a lightsaber or Force powers, can feel slow on repeat playthroughs.

🛠️ Recommended Mods (The Modernization Setup)
- Because the Steam version lacks native modern widescreen support and up-to-date graphic options, installing a few mods from platforms like Nexus Mods or DeadlyStream is crucial:
- KOTOR 1 Community Patch (K1CP): An absolute necessity that acts as an unofficial master fix, repairing hundreds of lingering gameplay bugs, broken quests, and clipping textures.
- Flawless Widescreen: An external tool used by the community to force the game into modern 1080p, 1440p, or ultrawide resolutions without stretching the HUD interface.
- KOTOR HD Overhaul (by Xarwynn): Completely updates the game's blurry 2003 environment, clothing, and weapon textures into crisp, high-definition models.
- High Quality Skyboxes (by Kexikus): Swaps out the original flat, pixelated space and planet backgrounds for beautiful, modern 3D planetary horizons.
